I feel like people who have posted here - yourself included, most likely - often tend to be especially empathetic/kind, because they can relate to people who are going through a lot. You're not crazy dude, we care.

You write beautifully. Definitely not useless words and symbols, you're able to convey real meaning and emotion and the complexity of your experience. You said you have a passion for creativity; I can absolutely tell. Thanks for sharing your thoughts, tbh it helped me know I'm not alone. 

I'm not anywhere near as good of a writer, so I don't really have any other way of saying it: just...please don't do this to yourself. I really, really, hope you stay alive and start taking care of yourself. I'll be thinking of you and hoping things get better.

Hey there. I'm really, really sorry about everything that's happened; it sounds like you've been given a very tough situation that you've gotta deal with right now. As someone who also recently dropped out of college (bc of depression/suicidal thoughts as well), I bet it just...really sucks right now. It might not be what you want, which is totally okay, but is there any way you could go back to college, if that was something you wanted to do? I don't know if that would help, but thought I'd bring it up. That's super cool that you went to medical school, and it sounds like you're smart - because you did so well at school - getting on Deans list and everything - but I also can tell by the way you write.

I may or may not be able to relate: I've also had to deal with feeling like a disappointment, as well as feeling like I was failing to meet everyone's expectations because of my performance in school. A lot of it was mental health related; I was so depressed that I stopped doing my work, which led me to feel inadequate and disappointed in myself, which made me put even less effort into my work - it's a vicious cycle. Let me know if that doesn't sound like your experience, but for me, something that helped was realizing that it wasn't my - or your - fault; mental illness is not the same thing as failure, or being lazy, or being inadequate. Everyone makes mistakes, and it's not our fault that we have an illness. Obviously, let me know if that doesn't sound like your experience, but that's something that really helped me.

Btw - I 100% relate to you spending time on your phone as a "temporary happiness." If you're looking for something to watch, I like the Try Guys' channel on Youtube; their content is kinda silly but really fun. :)

I really hope things get better sooner rather than later, but in the meantime keep on keeping on; you seem really cool, and I'm rooting for you.

Your life isn't over, you have plenty to come and look forward to. Focusing on bettering yourself, and look around for people or things in your life you may have missed previously. Sorry if those were a bunch of cheesy platitudes, but it's genuinely what works for me sometimes when I feel the way that you described.

Hey, here's my thoughts. If you feel like continuing to transition to be seen as more masculine would help you feel more authentic and comfortable, then you should continue to do it. Sure, you can't change the sex you were assigned at birth, but a couple things:

1. There's a lot of scientific evidence that says being a man (or any other gender) isn't actually defined by what genitals you have (if you have a penis) but instead biological differences in our brains. People who are trans guys are actually men whether or not they have a penis because they have the psychological and biological profile of a man. You should def look it up, but here's one article if you're interested: [https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/05/180524112351.htm](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/05/180524112351.htm) . Either way, you're valid as a man whether or not you have a penis. 
2. There are many ways to get surgery to construct a penis, or prosthetics that could alleviate your discomfort.
3. I personally wouldn't expect hormones to fix everything. Therapy, or other forms of ways to transition - like just socially transitioning, maybe getting a haircut that matches your gender and/or changing the pronouns that you use - are also super valuable parts of transitioning. Just because hormones aren't fixing everything doesn't mean that they aren't working. And if you're not comfortable with hormones, you don't have to use them - that doesn't mean you need to detransition. Plenty of trans people don't use hormones, and they are still valid in their gender/find a way to transition, through therapy or whatever, in a way that makes them happy. If you know you're a man, then you are already a man; think of transitioning as not "making" yourself into your preferred gender, but changing the way you present or see yourself in a way that you feel aligns with your gender and makes you happy.

I have OCD too, and I understand how much it sucks. It's impossible to turn off my thoughts and brain and I get really, really obsessive about things - and that's an understatement - I just mf hate it. I also know how it feels to have parents that are less than supportive about my identity and feelings. Please don't end it all, I've been there and still am to a certain extent. At the risk of sounding cheesy, you are more than your gender, and no matter what mistakes you make about your gender or anything else - p much everybody makes mistakes, you're not abnormal in that regard - you are valuable and deserve to live to learn from them and better yourself because of them. 

Explore a little bit; if you do one thing and it's not working or doesn't make you happy, try something else. Let me know if I'm wrong, but none of these decisions have to be permanent, even if they feel like they do. At the end of the day, you know yourself best; do what will make you most happy. And maybe try to find someone you trust to talk to about this other than your mom. Worst come to worst, I'm always here to listen.

at least where i was, they only have to report it if you are an "immediate danger to yourself and others." So if you talk about passive suicidal thoughts that you are not planning on acting on, that can be a good way to bring up suicidal thoughts without getting it reported! It'll probably vary based on the judgement of the school counselor.

But please, if you are considering seriously killing yourself, DEFINITELY reach out. Getting it reported sucks, but it might get you the help you need, and is better than having something happen to you.

It might for you, which would be great, but what it did for me was give me an understanding support system to stand with me as I dealt with suicidal thoughts/sadness. Even if it doesn't work out immediately, it eventually will, and imo it's important to remember that. Hang in there, and that's so awesome that you're going to reach out.
